title: How Portuguese works: the big picture
objectives: I can name the parts of speech and the basic terms of grammar (subject, object, infinitive, conjugation, person, number, tense, mood, agreement, gender, contraction) in English and Portuguese.
I can explain how a Portuguese sentence is built and where it differs from English: adjectives after the noun, no helper verb 'do', não before the verb and a dropped subject.
I can predict the gender of most nouns from their endings, form plurals, and make articles and adjectives agree with the noun.
I can explain how a verb is built from a stem and an ending that shows the person and number of the subject, and I know the map of tenses and moods the course will teach.
I can choose between você, o senhor, a senhora, a gente, nós and vocês, and I can tell when a preposition fuses with an article.

vocabulary.note: A noun names a person, place, thing or idea. Masculine, like most words in -o. The stress is on ti, so no written accent is needed. English 'substantive' is the same word, now rare; both come from Latin for a word that names a substance, a thing that exists in itself.
Masculine. Verbs are listed under their infinitive, which ends in -ar, -er or -ir.
The j sounds like the s in English 'measure'. An adjective describes a noun and agrees with it.

In most of Brazil the t before i sounds like English 'ch', so the ti of artigo is close to 'chee'. The articles are the small words o, a, os, as, um, uma. In the example, são means 'are' (the plural of é, 'is').
A pronoun stands in for a noun: pro- means 'for' and nome means 'name', so it is a word used in place of a name. Masculine, with the stress on no.
A preposition is a word placed before (pre-) another word to link it to the sentence. Feminine, because nouns in -ção are feminine. The plural is preposições, since -ção becomes -ções.
Singular means one. Grammar also uses it for the form of a word that means one.

example.pt: O singular de casas é casa.
example.en: The singular of casas is casa.

vocabulary.note: Plural means more than one. The plural of plural is plurais, by the rule that -al becomes -ais.

example.pt: O plural de casa é casas.
example.en: The plural of casa is casas.

vocabulary.note: An adjective in -o, so it has four forms: masculino, masculina, masculinos, masculinas.
The example shows agreement: the adjective is feminina because the noun menina is feminine.
Ends in -e, which gives no clue to gender, so learn it with its article: a frase.
Written o and pronounced like a short 'oo'. Used before a masculine singular noun; English 'the' has no gender, which is the difference. The plural is os.
Used before a feminine singular noun. The plural is as. The same spelling is also a preposition meaning 'to'; the job it does in the sentence tells you which.
The final unstressed e is said like 'ee' and the d before it softens to a j sound, so de is close to English 'jee'. Shows possession and origin. With an article it fuses: de + o = do, de + a = da.

The m is not pronounced as a closed-lip m: it makes the vowel nasal, roughly English 'ayn' said through the nose. Shows position. With an article it fuses: em + o = no, em + a = na. The example uses está, a form of estar, 'to be' for location, which note 6 explains.

The u is silent after q, and the unstressed e is a weak sound, roughly 'kee'. As a conjunction it links a second clause to the first. The example uses acha, from achar, which means 'to think' and literally 'to find'.

example.pt: Ana acha que a casa é bonita.
example.en: Ana thinks that the house is pretty.
example.literal: Ana finds that the house is pretty

vocabulary.note: Pronounced like English 'ee'. It is a different word from é, with the acute accent, which means 'is'.
The tilde makes ão a nasal diphthong, close to English 'now' said through the nose, with no n or g sound at the end. As 'not' it stands directly before the verb.

dialogues.title: A new house, a new cat
dialogues.context: Ana shows her friend Pedro her new house. Watch for adjectives that follow the noun and change their ending to agree with it: casa nova but carro novo, gato preto but gata preta. New forms: tenho is from ter, 'to have'; mas means 'but'; ele stands for the masculine noun gato and ela for the feminine gata; são is the plural of é. A question is just a statement with rising intonation, and the subject is left out in É pequena.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Oi, Pedro! Eu tenho uma casa nova.
lines.en: Hi, Pedro! I have a new house.
lines.literal: Hi, Pedro! I have a house new.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: A casa é grande?
lines.en: Is the house big?
lines.literal: The house is big?

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Não, a casa não é grande. É pequena.
lines.en: No, the house is not big. It is small.
lines.literal: No, the house not is big. Is small.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: E o carro é novo?
lines.en: And is the car new?
lines.literal: And the car is new?

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Não, o carro é velho. Mas eu tenho um gato e uma gata.
lines.en: No, the car is old. But I have a male cat and a female cat.
lines.literal: No, the car is old. But I have a cat and a she-cat.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: Ele é preto?
lines.en: Is he black?
lines.literal: He is black?

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Ele é preto e ela é branca.
lines.en: He is black and she is white.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: Eles são bonitos!
lines.en: They are pretty!

dialogues.title: Who speaks English?
dialogues.context: Lucas visits his friend Bia and meets her grandmother, dona Clara. He says você to Bia and a senhora to the older woman; both take the same verb form, fala. The subject is often dropped: moro, falo, comemos. New words: aqui is 'here', sim is 'yes', vovó is 'grandma' (the acute accent marks the stressed last syllable), um pouco is 'a little', com a gente is 'with us'. Verbs: fala is from falar, 'to speak'; mora and moro are from morar, 'to live'; come and comemos are from comer, 'to eat'.

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.pt: Oi, Bia! Você mora aqui?
lines.en: Hi, Bia! Do you live here?
lines.literal: Hi, Bia! You live here?

lines.speaker: Bia
lines.pt: Moro, sim. A vovó mora aqui com a gente.
lines.en: Yes, I do. Grandma lives here with us.
lines.literal: I-live, yes. The grandma lives here with the people.

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.pt: Dona Clara, a senhora fala inglês?
lines.en: Dona Clara, do you speak English?
lines.literal: Dona Clara, the lady speaks English?

lines.speaker: Clara
lines.pt: Não, eu não falo inglês. Mas a Bia fala.
lines.en: No, I do not speak English. But Bia does.
lines.literal: No, I not speak English. But the Bia speaks.

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.pt: Bia, você fala inglês?
lines.en: Bia, do you speak English?
lines.literal: Bia, you speak English?

lines.speaker: Bia
lines.pt: Falo um pouco. E você?
lines.en: I speak a little. And you?
lines.literal: I-speak a little. And you?

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.pt: Eu falo um pouco.
lines.en: I speak a little.

lines.speaker: Clara
lines.pt: Vocês comem aqui?
lines.en: Do you all eat here?
lines.literal: You-plural eat here?

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.pt: Comemos, sim. A gente come aqui.
lines.en: Yes, we do. We eat here.
lines.literal: We-eat, yes. The people eats here.

dialogues.title: Whose is it?
dialogues.context: Rita and Davi talk about who owns what and where people are. Watch for prepositions fusing with articles: da Ana (de + a), do Pedro (de + o), no Brasil (em + o), numa casa (em + uma), na escola (em + a), pela escola (por + a). New words: quem is 'who', onde is 'where', livro is 'book', escola is 'school', passar is 'to pass'; mora is from morar, 'to live', está is from estar, 'to be' (note 6), and vou is from ir, 'to go' (note 6).

lines.speaker: Rita
lines.pt: De quem é o livro?
lines.en: Whose is the book?
lines.literal: Of whom is the book?

lines.speaker: Davi
lines.pt: O livro é da Ana.
lines.en: The book is Ana's.
lines.literal: The book is of-the Ana.

lines.speaker: Rita
lines.pt: E o gato é da Ana?
lines.en: And is the cat Ana's?
lines.literal: And the cat is of-the Ana?

lines.speaker: Davi
lines.pt: Não, o gato é do Pedro.
lines.en: No, the cat is Pedro's.
lines.literal: No, the cat is of-the Pedro.

lines.speaker: Rita
lines.pt: O Pedro mora no Brasil?
lines.en: Does Pedro live in Brazil?
lines.literal: The Pedro lives in-the Brazil?

lines.speaker: Davi
lines.pt: Mora, sim. Ele mora numa casa pequena.
lines.en: Yes, he does. He lives in a small house.
lines.literal: Lives, yes. He lives in-a house small.

lines.speaker: Rita
lines.pt: E a Ana, onde está?
lines.en: And Ana, where is she?
lines.literal: And the Ana, where is?

lines.speaker: Davi
lines.pt: Ela está na escola. Você passa pela escola?
lines.en: She is at school. Do you pass by the school?
lines.literal: She is in-the school. You pass by-the school?

lines.speaker: Rita
lines.pt: Passo, sim. Vou falar com ela.
lines.en: Yes, I do. I am going to talk to her.
lines.literal: I-pass, yes. I-go to-speak with her.

grammar.title: Parts of speech and the vocabulary of grammar
grammar.explanation:
Grammar is the description of how words are built and combined into sentences. To describe it you need names for the kinds of word and for the jobs words do to each other. This note defines those names once, because every later lesson uses them. Portuguese has the same parts of speech as English (this course counts nine), so none of the categories is foreign. What differs is how the words behave, and the next notes show that.

A part of speech is a class of words that do the same job in a sentence. The table defines the nine classes. One spelling can belong to different classes, and the job it does in the sentence decides: Portuguese a is an article in 'a casa' (the house) and a preposition meaning 'to' in other sentences.

Terms about the sentence. A sentence is a frase. The subject is the person or thing that performs the action or is described: in 'Ana eats the bread', Ana is the subject. The object is the person or thing that receives the action: 'the bread'.

Terms about verbs. The infinitive is the dictionary form of a verb, with no subject and no time: 'to speak' in English, falar in Portuguese. To conjugate a verb is to change its form so that it shows who is acting, and the full set of forms is its conjugation. Person says who acts: the first person is the speaker (I, we), the second person is the one spoken to (you), the third person is anyone else (he, she, it, they). Number says whether there is one (singular) or more than one (plural). A tense tells when the action happens: present, past or future. A mood tells how the speaker regards the action: as a plain fact, as something wished for or doubtful, or as a command.

Terms about nouns. Gender is a class, masculine or feminine, which every Portuguese noun belongs to. Agreement is the rule that the words attached to a noun, its article and its adjectives, must copy its gender and number. A contraction is two words fused into one, like English 'do not' becoming 'don't'. Portuguese contracts prepositions with articles, for example de + o becoming do. Notes 3 to 7 work each of these ideas out in detail.

Worked through. In 'A menina fala', a is an article, menina a noun and the subject, fala a verb. In 'A menina pequena fala muito', pequena is an adjective describing menina and muito is an adverb telling how much. In 'Ela fala com Ana e com Pedro', ela is a pronoun standing for a noun, com is a preposition and e is a conjunction joining two phrases. In 'Oi! Ana come o pão', oi is an interjection, Ana is the subject, come the verb and o pão the object. Falar is an infinitive, and falo, fala and falamos are conjugated forms of that one verb.

Literal lines. Next to a natural English translation, this course often shows a literal line: the Portuguese words rendered one by one, in Portuguese word order, so that you can see what the words actually say. English words joined by hyphens stand for one Portuguese word (of-the for do, I-speak for falo). The natural translation tells you what an English speaker would say; the literal line tells you how Portuguese builds the idea; the notes tell you when to use it.

rows: names a person, place, thing or idea
small word before a noun; marks it as a specific or a non-specific one
an action, state or event; its form changes
tells how, when, where or how much
links a noun to the rest of the sentence: place, origin, possession

examples.en: The small girl talks a lot.

examples.pt: Ela fala com Ana e com Pedro.
examples.en: She talks with Ana and with Pedro.

grammar.title: Word order, questions and negation
grammar.explanation:
Every language needs a way to show who does what to whom. English does it mainly with word order, because English nouns never change form: 'Ana sees Pedro' and 'Pedro sees Ana' differ only in the position of the names. Portuguese nouns do not change form either, so Portuguese also relies on the neutral order subject, verb, object: 'Ana vê Pedro'. That part is the same. Three things are different.

First, adjectives usually come after the noun they describe. 'A casa grande' is literally 'the house big'. The default position is after the noun, and it is the normal position for colours, shapes, nationalities and other factual descriptions. A small group of common adjectives, such as bom (good), mau (bad), grande (big), novo (new) and velho (old), may also stand before the noun, and then they usually express the speaker's opinion or a figurative sense: 'um grande amigo' is a great friend, while 'um amigo grande' is a big, tall friend. Numbers, quantity words and possessive words such as meu (my), muitos (many) and dois (two) go before the noun.

Second, Portuguese has no helper verb like English 'do'. English needs 'do' to make a question ('Does she speak?') and a negative ('She does not speak'), and the main verb then loses its ending. Portuguese changes neither the verb nor its position. A yes-or-no question is the plain statement said with rising intonation at the end and written with a question mark: 'Ela fala.' becomes 'Ela fala?' A question with a question word puts that word first: onde (where), como (how), quem (who), o que (what), quando (when), por que (why). To make a negative, put não directly before the verb: 'Ela não fala.' Portuguese also allows extra negative words in the same sentence, so 'Ela não fala nada' (she does not say anything) is standard, not a mistake.

Third, the subject is often left out, because the verb ending already shows who is acting. 'Falo' can only mean 'I speak', whereas English 'speak' alone would fit several subjects. Note 5 explains how far Brazilians take this.

Worked through. In 'Ana come o pão', Ana is the subject, come the verb and o pão the object, in the same order as English. In 'Você fala português?' nothing translates English 'do'; only the rising intonation and the question mark mark it as a question. In 'Eu não falo inglês', não sits directly before falo. In 'Onde a Ana mora?', the question word comes first and the rest is the ordinary statement order.

grammar.title: Gender, number and agreement
grammar.explanation:
Gender is a class that every noun belongs to: masculine or feminine. There is no neuter class. The gender of a thing is a fact about its word, not about the thing: a table is feminine (a mesa) and a book is masculine (o livro) for no reason of meaning. For people and animals the gender normally follows the sex, so menino is a boy and menina a girl, but it remains a property of the word: a pessoa (the person) is feminine even when the person is a man. English keeps a trace of gender only in the pronouns he, she and it.

Most genders can be predicted from the ending; the table lists the dependable ones. Exceptions worth knowing: a few nouns in -o are feminine (a mão, the hand; a foto and a moto, short for fotografia and motocicleta), and a few in -a are masculine (o dia, the day; o mapa, the map; o planeta, the planet). Nouns in -ma that come from Greek are masculine (o problema, o sistema, o programa), but other words in -ma follow the ordinary -a rule (a cama, the bed). Nouns in -or are masculine except a few such as a flor, a cor and a dor (flower, colour, pain). The ending -ão is split: -ção and -são give feminine nouns (a canção, a televisão), with the rare exception o coração. Many other -ão nouns are masculine (o pão, o irmão, o avião), but some are feminine (a mão, a razão, a questão). For endings not in the table, such as -e, -l and -z, there is no reliable rule (o leite but a noite), so the safe habit is to learn every noun together with its article: a cidade, never just cidade.

Number is singular or plural. English adds -s almost always; Portuguese spells the plural according to the last sound of the singular, as the table shows. Two details: a stressed -el or -ol takes an acute accent in the plural (papel, papéis), and the accent of português disappears in portugueses, because the default stress rule now gives the right syllable. The three plurals of nouns in -ão are a historical accident and must be learned word by word: most are -ões, a few are -ães and a few are -ãos.

Agreement is the heart of this system. A noun fixes a gender and a number, and every article and adjective attached to it must show the same gender and number. The definite articles ('the') are o, a, os, as. The indefinite articles ('a', 'an', 'some') are um, uma, uns, umas. An adjective in -o has four forms (novo, nova, novos, novas); most adjectives in -e or a consonant have one form for both genders and only add the plural (grande, grandes; azul, azuis). Adjectives in -ês, -ol or -or, including those of nationality, are an exception and add -a for the feminine (português, portuguesa; espanhol, espanhola; trabalhador, trabalhadora). Agreement holds wherever the adjective stands, including after the verb: 'A casa é pequena', 'As casas são pequenas'. A mixed group takes the masculine plural: a boy and a girl are 'altos'.

For people, the usual pairing swaps the ending: menino and menina, amigo and amiga, filho and filha, gato and gata. Nouns in -or add -a (professor, professora), nouns in -ês become -esa (português, portuguesa), and nouns in -e often keep one form and change only the article (o estudante, a estudante). A few pairs are different words (o homem, a mulher; o pai, a mãe).

Worked through. In 'o gato preto', the article, the noun and the adjective all say masculine singular; in 'os gatos pretos' all three say masculine plural, and in 'as gatas pretas' all three say feminine plural. Nothing is optional: 'os gatos preto' is wrong. In 'A cidade é grande e o problema é pequeno', cidade is feminine (-dade) and problema is masculine (-ma from Greek); grande has one form for both genders, while pequeno takes -o to agree with problema. In 'Os meninos e as meninas são altos', a mixed group takes the masculine plural. In 'As canções são bonitas', canção is feminine (-ção) and its plural is canções. In 'O professor e a professora são brasileiros', the pair swaps -or for -ora.

grammar.title: Verbs: infinitive, conjugation, tense and mood
grammar.explanation:
A Portuguese verb is listed under its infinitive, and every regular infinitive ends in -ar, -er or -ir. Those endings sort the verbs into three families, called conjugations in traditional grammar: falar (to speak), comer (to eat) and partir (to leave). A regular verb follows the pattern of its family, so learning the pattern once unlocks thousands of verbs. (There is also pôr, to put, with its relatives, which is irregular.)

To conjugate a verb, remove the family ending to find the stem (fal-, com-, part-) and add an ending that shows the person and number of the subject. English does this in one slot only (I speak, she speaks). Portuguese does it in every slot, so the ending alone tells you who is acting, and this is why the subject pronoun can be dropped. The table shows the present tense of the three families.

The traditional system has six slots: first, second and third person, each singular and plural. In Brazil the system is reduced. The second person plural vós is archaic and survives only in old texts and prayers; vocês (you, more than one) takes the third person plural instead. The second person singular tu is regional (note 5), and the everywhere form for 'you' is você, which takes the third person singular. So in speech there are really four forms: the eu form, the third person singular shared by você, ele, ela and a gente, the nós form, and the third person plural shared by vocês, eles and elas. Speakers often go further and replace the nós form with a gente plus the third person singular.

A tense tells when something happens and a mood tells how the speaker regards it. The indicative mood states facts, and it holds most of the tenses this course builds: the present (falo, I speak), the preterite (falei, I spoke, a completed action), the imperfect (falava, I used to speak or I was speaking), the progressive (estou falando, I am speaking right now), the future (vou falar, I am going to speak, and falarei, I will speak), the conditional (falaria, I would speak) and the compound tenses that use the helper verb ter (tenho falado, I have been speaking; tinha falado, I had spoken). The subjunctive mood expresses what is wished for, doubted or not yet real; it has a present (que eu fale), an imperfect (se eu falasse) and a future (quando eu falar). The imperative mood gives commands (fale!). The personal infinitive is an infinitive that takes an ending for its own subject (para eles falarem), which English does not have.

This is a map, not an assignment. The beginner lessons (A1) use mainly the present, with ir plus an infinitive for the near future and a few fixed phrases from other tenses. The preterite, imperfect, progressive, simple future, conditional and imperative are taught properly at the elementary level (A2), and the compound tenses, the subjunctive and the personal infinitive at the intermediate levels (B1 and B2).

Worked through. In 'Eu falo português', falo is the stem fal- plus -o, the first person singular ending. One third person singular form, fala, serves ele, ela and você. In 'Nós comemos e eles partem', the endings -mos and -m mark the first and third person plural. The colloquial a gente takes the third person singular verb, which fits its literal meaning 'the people' (a third person noun). Vocês takes the third person plural. Falar, comer and partir are each an infinitive, one from each family.

examples.pt: Ele fala, ela fala, você fala.
examples.en: He speaks, she speaks, you speak.

examples.pt: Falar, comer e partir são verbos.
examples.en: To speak, to eat and to leave are verbs.

grammar.title: Subject pronouns and forms of address
grammar.explanation:
A subject pronoun stands in for the noun that is the subject of the verb. The forms are eu (I), você (you, one person), ele (he), ela (she), nós (we), a gente (we, in everyday speech), vocês (you, more than one), eles (they, masculine or mixed) and elas (they, feminine). There is no word for 'it' as a subject: a thing takes ele or ela according to its gender when a pronoun is needed at all, and usually the subject is simply left out, so 'É bonito' means 'It is pretty' and 'Chove' means 'It is raining'. Você is stressed on the last syllable, which is not the default for a word ending in a vowel, so an accent is written; the circumflex, as the lesson on accents explained, shows that the e is closed. It sounds like vo-SAY, with the e held steady without the glide of English 'say', and with the first o weak and short, sometimes close to u.

Why does você take the third person verb? Você began as a respectful way of addressing someone, Vossa Mercê, 'Your Mercy', a noun phrase about the listener spoken in the third person, like English 'Your Majesty is welcome'. Over time it shrank through vosmecê to você, but it kept its third person verb. So você names the person you are speaking to while being grammatically third person. The same holds for o senhor and a senhora, which literally mean 'the gentleman' and 'the lady'. The result in Brazil is that ele, ela, você and a gente all use one verb form.

This has a consequence for the dropped subject. The eu and nós forms have endings of their own (falo, falamos), so eu and nós are dropped freely. But fala could be about him, her, you or us, so Brazilians usually keep the pronoun unless the context already makes the subject clear. Compare Spanish or European Portuguese, where more forms are distinct and the pronoun is dropped more often.

Choosing 'you' is a choice of relationship. Você is the neutral everyday form for one person, used with friends, colleagues and strangers. O senhor (to a man) and a senhora (to a woman) are more respectful and used with older people, in formal service situations and in official settings. Tu, the old second person singular, is used in parts of Brazil, including the south, parts of the north and northeast and some speakers in Rio de Janeiro. The verb that goes with tu varies by region: tu falas with the -s ending in some places, and tu fala, the third person singular, in many others. A learner can understand tu and never produce it, because você is correct everywhere. For more than one person, vocês is used in every register, and os senhores and as senhoras are the formal plurals. Formality changes only which word you choose and the tone around it; the verb stays in the third person for all of them.

Worked through. The first three examples all mean 'Do you speak English?' and all use fala; only the word for 'you' changes, and the literal lines show why: você is the neutral everyday form, while o senhor and a senhora literally say 'the gentleman' and 'the lady', a respectful way to address someone in the third person. A gente fala is the everyday 'we' and nós falamos the written or careful one. Vocês falam asks the question of several people. Elas moram aqui is about women only, and takes the third person plural moram.

grammar.title: Ser, estar, ter and ir: four irregular workhorses
grammar.explanation:
A regular verb follows the stem plus ending pattern of its family. An irregular verb breaks the pattern, so its forms must be learned one by one. Irregular verbs are not random. They are the most frequent verbs in the language, and the most frequent words keep the oldest and most changed forms, just as English keeps am, is, are, was and went for its commonest verbs. Four of them do a great deal of work in Portuguese, and you will meet them in the first lessons, so here is the overview. Each one gets its own lesson later.

Ser and estar both translate English 'to be', but Portuguese divides the job. Ser says what something is: identity, origin, profession and lasting characteristics (Ana é alta, Ana is tall; eu sou brasileiro, I am Brazilian). Estar says how or where something is now: location and conditions that can change (Ana está cansada, Ana is tired; o livro está em casa, the book is at home). Ter means 'to have' (ela tem uma casa), and in everyday Brazilian speech it also means 'there is': 'Tem café' is 'There is coffee.' Ir means 'to go', and ir plus an infinitive makes a future that matches English 'going to': 'Vou falar' is 'I am going to speak'.

The table gives the present. The forms for você, ele, ela and a gente are again one form, and vocês, eles and elas share one. The plural of ter is written têm, with a circumflex, to tell it from the singular tem; in Brazilian speech the two are pronounced alike.

Worked through. 'Eu sou brasileiro e estou aqui' uses ser for origin and estar for location. 'Ela é alta e está cansada' uses ser for a lasting trait and estar for a passing state. 'Tem café em casa' uses tem for 'there is' and, literally, says 'has coffee in house'. 'Eu vou falar com Ana' is vou plus the infinitive falar. 'Elas vão para casa' uses vão, the third person plural of ir; para casa is literally 'to house', without any article.

examples.pt: Eu sou brasileiro e estou aqui.
examples.en: I am Brazilian and I am here.

examples.pt: Ela é alta e está cansada.
examples.en: She is tall and she is tired.
I am going to talk to Ana.

grammar.title: Prepositions and contractions
grammar.explanation:
A preposition is a short word placed before a noun or pronoun to show how it relates to the rest of the sentence: place, origin, possession, direction, purpose or company. The six commonest in Portuguese are de (of, from), em (in, on, at), a (to, at), por (by, through, for), para (to, for, in order to) and com (with).

English keeps the preposition and the article as separate words: 'of the', 'in the', 'to the'. Portuguese fuses them into a single word when a preposition meets an article. This is a contraction. It is not optional, unlike English 'do not' and 'don't': in ordinary phrases like these 'de o' is simply wrong and must be written and said do. The table shows the pattern. The accent in a + a = à is the grave accent of the accents lesson, which marks that two a sounds have merged into one; a + o gives ao without an accent.

Two prepositions do not fuse: para and com stay separate (para o, com a). In quick speech para is shortened to pra and para o to pro, but for now write para. A contraction happens only when there is an article to fuse with: 'em casa' (at home) and 'de Ana' have no article, so nothing fuses. Place names show this. Some take an article (o Brasil, o Rio de Janeiro), giving 'no Brasil', while others take none (Portugal, São Paulo), giving 'em Portugal'. First names in Brazilian speech often take an article too (a Ana, o Pedro), which is why you hear 'da Ana' and 'do Pedro'; 'de Ana' is also correct.

The indefinite articles contract as well: em + um = num, em + uma = numa, de + um = dum and de + uma = duma. In Brazil num and numa are normal in speech and writing, while dum and duma are rare and old-fashioned, and 'de um' and 'de uma' are the usual spelling. Finally, de and em also fuse with some pronouns: de + ele = dele (his) and em + ela = nela (in her).

Worked through. The literal lines show that Portuguese says 'in-the Brazil' and 'in-the school' where English drops the article, and that it says 'of-the Pedro' where English says 'Pedro's'. Do, da, no, na, à, pela and numa are each a preposition fused with an article (de + o, de + a, em + o, em + a, a + a, por + a, em + uma). Com stays separate: 'com o Pedro'.

examples.en: I live in a small house.

culture.title: First names, titles and the many ways to say 'you'
culture.text:
Brazilians move to first names very quickly, even with people they have just met and even at work. Polite handles are built on the first name rather than the surname: seu João, dona Maria, and doutor or doutora for professionals such as doctors and lawyers. The formal 'you', o senhor and a senhora, is kept for people who are clearly older or of higher standing, for formal service situations and for official settings. Using você with a stranger is normal and is not rude.

Which word for 'you' you hear depends on where you are. Você is the standard in large parts of the country, including São Paulo and Minas Gerais. Tu is heard in the south, in parts of the north and the northeast, and among some speakers in Rio de Janeiro, sometimes mixed with você and with varying verb endings. Because você is understood and accepted everywhere, it is the safe default for a learner.

Written and spoken Portuguese also differ. In conversation a gente very often replaces nós, and short forms such as pra for para and tá for está are everywhere. In this course they are introduced in informal dialogue only when they have been explained.

exercises.prompt: Match the Portuguese grammar word with its English meaning
exercises.explanation: The Portuguese names are close to the English ones, but each carries its own gender: o substantivo, a preposição.

exercises.prompt: In the sentence 'A menina fala.', which word is the verb?
exercises.explanation: Fala is the third person singular of falar. A is an article and menina is the noun.

exercises.prompt: What part of speech is 'pequena' in 'a casa pequena'?
exercises.explanation: Pequena describes casa, follows it, and ends in -a to agree with the feminine noun.

exercises.prompt: In 'Ana e Pedro moram em casa', which word is a preposition?
exercises.explanation: Em (in, at) links casa to the verb. The word e is a conjunction.
Stem fal- plus -o, the first person singular ending of the -ar family.
Eles moram is the third person plural; no is em + o.
Nouns in -ma from Greek are masculine (o problema). Casa ends in -a, canção in -ção and cidade in -dade, which are all feminine.
Nouns in -dade are feminine (a cidade). Livro and carro end in -o, and problema is a masculine noun in -ma.
Cidade ends in -dade, so it is feminine and takes the article a.

exercises.hint_en: The house is small. (base form: pequeno)
exercises.explanation: Casa is feminine singular, so the adjective takes -a.

exercises.hint_en: The cats are black. (base form: preto)
exercises.explanation: Gatos is masculine plural, so the adjective takes -os.
Pequena means small and follows casa; nova means new and comes after é.

exercises.prompt: Which subject can NOT go with the verb form 'fala'?
exercises.explanation: Fala is the third person singular. With eu the verb is falo.
Stem com- plus -emos, the nós ending of the -er family.
Vocês takes the third person plural ending -am.

exercises.prompt: In 'Ela come o pão e ele fala', which word is a conjunction?
exercises.explanation: E joins two clauses. Ela is a pronoun, o an article and come a verb.

exercises.prompt: English says 'She does not speak.' Portuguese says 'Ela não fala.' What takes the place of English 'does'?
choices: Nothing: não before the verb is enough
exercises.explanation: Portuguese has no helper verb for questions or negatives. Não goes directly before the verb.

exercises.prompt: Which is the literal, word-for-word rendering of 'a casa grande'?
exercises.explanation: The literal rendering keeps Portuguese word order: article, noun, adjective. The natural English translation, 'the big house', reverses the last two words.

exercises.prompt: 'O livro é do Pedro' is literally 'the book is of-the Pedro'. Which natural English translation matches?
choices: The book is from the Pedro
exercises.explanation: De marks possession, and do is de + o. English says Pedro's, with no article.

exercises.prompt: Which two words does the contraction 'ao' combine?
exercises.explanation: Ao is a + o. The combination a + a is written à.

exercises.hint_en: The book is the boy's. (de + o)
exercises.explanation: The preposition de fuses with the article o: de + o = do.
The preposition a and the feminine article a merge into à, written with the grave accent. Para a is also correct but does not fuse.

exercises.prompt: Match each contraction with the words it fuses
exercises.explanation: A contraction is a preposition fused with the article that follows it.
Vai is ir, movement toward; à is a + a.

exercises.prompt: Which of the four irregular verbs says where something is right now?
exercises.explanation: Estar is for location and changing states. Ser is for identity and lasting traits.
The statement order with a question mark; there is no helper verb like 'does', and the verb is the third person singular fala.
The adjective follows the noun and agrees with it.

exercises.prompt_en: I do not have a cat.
exercises.explanation: Não stands directly before the verb tenho.
No helper verb; não goes before fala.
Both adjectives agree with the masculine noun carro and end in -o; the colour follows the noun.
Em + o = no, because Brasil takes the article o.
